messages.subject: How to stop ctmm from automatically loading upon startup
messages.subject_clean: How to stop ctmm from automatically loading upon startup
messages.body_plain: I have a script that first uses commands from the OpenStreetMap package to create maps of location data, then the ctmm package to calculate home range sizes. The ctmm package interferes with OpenStreetMap, so I have to load ctmm after I run the OpenStreetMap code. The issue is that R keeps automatically loading ctmm as soon as I open the program. Once ctmm has automatically loaded, I can't successfully run my script without uninstalling ctmm so it won't automatically load again, and then close out of R before restarting it. Simply offloading the ctmm package won't work for some reason, I have to uninstall it every time it's automatically loaded. As per an online forum, I tried going to tools>global options>restore .RData into workspace at startup and unchecking this option, though the ctmm package continues to automatically load every time. Does anyone have any suggestions for how to prevent the ctmm package from automatically loading every time I open R? Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: Coming up with IID for FIT summary
messages.subject_clean: Coming up with IID for FIT summary
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michela,

Either your data are too coarse to estimate diffusion rates, or (if some locations are sampled close together in time) you need a location-error model. But the IID model is pretty common with coarsely sampled VHF data.

When you have an IID model, akde() returns the bias-corrected GRF KDE: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.12673
which is a fancier KDE method, and you can also include boundaries and habitat selection parameters.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: How to stop ctmm from automatically loading upon startup
messages.subject_clean: How to stop ctmm from automatically loading upon startup
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jason,

After stopping R from saving & loading workspaces, you probably just needed to restart in a new workspace.

For packages with namespace collision, you can use package::function() to call functions from that package without loading the package. This will work as long as the package exports all of their user-facing functions, though sometimes package developers will forget to export basic methods like plot() in their namespace.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: speed = 0, warning "Movement model is fractal"
messages.body_plain:
Hi Iran,

This is the advantage of working with continuous-time models. You can compare across sampling schedules, as shown by the mean estimate being constant as a function of sampling frequency: https://movementecologyjournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s40462-019-0177-1/figures/6
This holds until the sampling frequency becomes so low that you can barely resolve speed, and then you get some positive bias right before you can no longer estimate speed. But even then, you at least have wide confidence intervals to know that the estimates aren't very good.

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Johanne,

Currently in the rsf.fit(), NA values are treated as inaccessible areas. They can be present in the raster, but not where the data are, and ideally you want to limit them to either being in actual inaccessible areas or far from the data and UD. I recommend plotting your data atop the raster with plot(DATA,R=RASTER)to get a sense what you are dealing with. A lot of times people aren't using a big enough buffer area for their data.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Coming up with IID for FIT summary
messages.subject_clean: Coming up with IID for FIT summary
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michela,

You should use AKDE with the selected autocorrelation model. When the selected autocorrelation model is IID, then AKDE limits to the KDE implemented in ctmm. The same bias correction for GRF oversmoothing is present in both, and the optimal weights for IID data limit to uniform weights. So you can state that you used optimally weighted AKDE, and some of the selected autocorrelation models were IID.

There is habitat selection in ctmm via rsf.fit(), and now rsf.select(),  which adjusts for the autocorrelation, and estimates (rather than fixes) the available area, and automates an appropriate number of available points: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
which can take categorical variables, and you can also get the population selection with mean(). This is what I would recommend for range resident populations, and I would recommend integrated SSFs for analyzing non-resident populations like migrations.

But you can also export to raster, sp, and sf objects: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/export.html
and from there it should be straightforward to get your outputs into other packages.

Best,
Chris

> > > > > >
> > > > > > Informative prior parameters should give credible intervals that approximate the unknown prediction intervals of the population. So, in this case, GPS devices usually have a location error that ranges from a few meters to 10-20 meters at HDOP=1, and your credible intervals should reflect that. There are a number of GPS devices tested in https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.06.12.130195v2.full
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I suppose you could compare AIC with and without HDOP as long as the two priors were comparable. You can also see if your autocorrelation timescales increase (they decrease with unaccounted-for location error).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Large home-range CIs either mean that the individual isn't range resident or that the duration of tracking data is very short.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Statistical efficiency of home-range estimation versus effective sample size is discussed here: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.13270
> > > > > >
> > > > > > When you have a nesting area and foraging area very far apart like that, that violates the stationary assumption of the base models. You would want to segment the data, estimate separate ranges, and then combine them with mean() or pkde() depending on what the areas correspond to.

> > > > > >

> > > > > >

> > > > > > Diffusion rate is a measure of variance from an initial location over time, and will be explained in an upcoming manuscript. But it is an alternative metric for movement activity, when you don't have data that are good enough for speed/distance estimation.

messages.subject: rsf.select
messages.body_plain:
Dear community,

New in the development version of the ctmm package is the rsf.select() function, which you can install via:
remotes::install_github("ctmm-initiative/ctmm")
and then see the associated help file in:
?rsf.select

rsf.select() will perform model selection on multiple formula terms or raster covariates. This is recommended when using mean() to estimate population-level parameters, as, otherwise, unsupported parameter estimates can have ill-conditioned COV matrices, which mean() requires for calculation. Importantly, mean() does not require the same parameters to be selected on all individuals.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: [ctmm-user] Estimating population level UD
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dibyendu,

There are several ways people have classified movement behaviors. I have done this with elk GPS collar data in Wyoming using a combination of a couple methods.

I first used net square displacement (nsd() function in the amt package) to determine migratory start and end dates for both spring migration and fall migration. Because you only want to use periods of range residency to run through akde() and pkde(), nsd() can help you figure out what GPS data to not run through.

Then I used a spatiotemporal segmentation method to further check the results of the nsd() dates. I used the package segclus2D (you can read more about it here: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1365-2656.13105 ).

I’m sure there are other ways people have classified movement behavior- but these two have worked well for me. I also visually inspected the results of nsd() and segclus2d(), to triple check. Especially because the elk I study don’t always have straightforward migratory and range resident periods.

Hope this helps!
Avery

You do want to segment the data if the autocorrelation structure of the different behaviors differs greatly, because the current models in the package are stationary. Afterwards, you can always re-combine the different UDs with mean().

Hi Dibyendu,
I did something similar with New World Vultures. I used migration mapper (https://migrationinitiative.org/content/migration-mapper, https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13976) to identify outbound and return migrations. Migration mapper uses a NSD to visualize and help you to identify the seasons. This is the same analysis that Avery mentioned. Migration mapper has a very friendly user interface and it returns a table with the start and end dates of each season. It also returns shapefiles with animal fixes classified for each season. While processing the data in migration mapper you can add additional information on behavior to each individual. Migration mapper now integrates ctmm.

My $0.02, hope it helps. All the best,

Adrian

messages.subject: Re: [ctmm-user] Re: suitability from rsf.fit
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ryan,

suitability() calculated from the mean() RSF would correspond to the suitability of the mean animal, while averaging the individual suitabilities would correspond to the mean suitability of the population. The two calculations are not the same unless the population variance is very low.

Right now I'm working on including the uncertainty in the suitability() output. After that, I could put together a mean suitability function if people want that.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject_clean: Optimizing the TPEQD projection in CTMM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris!

Can you elaborate on how CTMM optimizes the Two Point Equidistant projection?  I combed thru some of the code on GitHub but couldn't find anything.

I do believe it is the optimal projection for my study area as  I compared the distortion on distance calculations across several projections and the TPEQD projection performed the best. However, I would like to understand how ctmm comes to this dataset-specific specification of the projection, specifically how are the "two points" are chosen. Are these optimized to reduce error?

For my work, I coerced my data (in WGS84) into a large MoveStack, and then used as.telemetry() to coerce it into a list of telemetry objects.
Examining the projection info for each object shows they are all the same.

DATA.trj[[1]]@info$projection
"+proj=tpeqd +lat_1=64.2001964300436 +lon_1=-112.523229163276 +lat_2=65.7643765449217 +lon_2=-111.041601376637 +x_0=0 +y_0=0 +datum=WGS84 +units=m +no_defs"

When I plot these lat_1,long_1 & lat_2, long2, they are somewhat central to the entire dataset (screenshot shows them overtop of the telemetry dataset of ~300 hundred caribous over several years).  How does CTMM pick these points?

Thanks, Robin

messages.subject: Re: Optimizing the TPEQD projection in CTMM
messages.subject_clean: Optimizing the TPEQD projection in CTMM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Robin,

I take the (x,y,z) locations in 3D Euclidean space (not constrained to the ellipsoid) and perform k=2 geometric median clustering with the Gmedian package, which is a form of clustering that is robust to outliers. I then take the two cluster medians and project them down to the ellipsoid (though, typically they won't be far from the ellipsoid). With multiple individuals, I do this once per individual and then again on all of the individual cluster locations to prevent over-fitting to the better sampled individuals. The code is in median.R: https://github.com/ctmm-initiative/ctmm/blob/master/R/median.R

With the TPEQD projection, distances from either focus are accurate. So, if you have a big migration, then the projection can still be relatively accurate. In cases like yours, where you don't have a big migration, then you just get two points in the bulk of the data. Usually these two points span the larger extent of the data, which is what you want.

Best,
Chris

> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > Many functions have a 'cores' argument if you are running on UNIX (Linux or Mac) that can be used to parallelize aspects of the computation, though it is almost always better to parallelize at the top level in your loop over individuals. Both ctmm.select() and optimizer() have a cores argument. If you are analyzing one individual on UNIX then control=list(cores=-1) could speed up the optimization considerably on a large dataset, as your 42k-point likelihood function then gets evaluated multiple times in parallel. messages.body_snippet:
Hi Adam,

The control list argument of ctmm.fit() and ctmm.select() is passed to ctmm's optimizer(). This can take a cores argument to speed up optimization on large datasets.
https://ctmm-initiative.

messages.subject: Re: Changes in sampling intervals
messages.body_plain:
Hi Adam,

I'm running everything in a regular for loop so that I can see the progress. foreach doesn't directly let you see the updates from every process running in parallel. Everything is progressing fine and at the speed that I would expect. I'm on the 4th model of the longest dataset, with the 2 largest models completed. In general, you can expect that 10x the data will result in 10x the computation time. Fitting with an error model like this will also take 3x longer than fitting without an error model, because more parameters are being optimized.

If you want to see progress inside a foreach loop, there are ways to do that: https://www.vikparuchuri.com/monitoring-progress-inside-foreach-loop/

Alternatively, with larger datasets like this, you can run a regular loop and parallelize the optimizer with control=list(cores=-1). This only works in UNIX (Linux or MacOS) and is only beneficial on larger datasets. On smaller datasets, this can get the process killed by the OS if processes are being forked too frequently.

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Adam,

I was just doing what you were, but with a regular for() loop.  I didn't keep running it, but I don't think the entire calculation would have taken me more than a day on the one core. If you are having problems with RStudio crashing, I would recommend running longer tasks from a script executed directly from the command line. But regardless of what's crashing, I would recommend incrementally saving your results to a file. That way you can have your script start by reading in that file and picking up where you left off.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Meta analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I'm starting to apply the meta-analysis within the ctmm to explore the variation in home range across groups (sex, life stage, behavior) and was wondering if it is ok to include all animals in my dataset, even the ones that do not show range-residency behavior?

And is it possible to include animals with several deployments as well? Semi-variograms look very strange when I use multiple deployments, so to run individual AKDE I used only the longest deployment available for each animal.

Thanks very much for all your support.

Best,

Iran

messages.subject: Re: Meta analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi Iran,

It depends on what you want your averages to represent and whether or not you have enough individuals in those categories to form a representative sample.

If you have multiple deployments on the same individual, then the variograms are going to suffer from the gaps. But as long as the animal is in the same area, then its okay to use all deployments at once.

Best,
Chris

> You should use AKDE with the selected autocorrelation model. When the selected autocorrelation model is IID, then AKDE limits to the KDE implemented in ctmm. The same bias correction for GRF oversmoothing is present in both, and the optimal weights for IID data limit to uniform weights. So you can state that you used optimally weighted AKDE, and some of the selected autocorrelation models were IID.
>
> There is habitat selection in ctmm via rsf.fit(), and now rsf.select(),  which adjusts for the autocorrelation, and estimates (rather than fixes) the available area, and automates an appropriate number of available points: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
> which can take categorical variables, and you can also get the population selection with mean(). This is what I would recommend for range resident populations, and I would recommend integrated SSFs for analyzing non-resident populations like migrations.
>
> But you can also export to raster, sp, and sf objects: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/export.html
> and from there it should be straightforward to get your outputs into other packages.
>
> Best,
> Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Michela,

There is an example of how to assign a prior for the location error distribution at the end of vignette('error'): https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/articles/error.html
You can make it so that your credible intervals contain 3m error at low HDOP values.

The default methods should be good down to effective sample sizes of 4-5. I would consider an effective sample size over 20 to be pretty good.

Best,
Chris

The same bias correction for GRF oversmoothing is present in both, and the optimal weights for IID data limit to uniform weights. So you can state that you used optimally weighted AKDE, and some of the selected autocorrelation models were IID.
> >

> > which can take categorical variables, and you can also get the population selection with mean(). This is what I would recommend for range resident populations, and I would recommend integrated SSFs for analyzing non-resident populations like migrations.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Iran,

occurrence() is not really something to compare because it is not a biological parameter. Using the output of occurrence() to get a point estimate on habitat used would be a comparable statistic.

That sounds like an error message from a different package. Try either running ctmm::meta() or not loading any other packages (and that includes loading your working environment). If the problem persists, then you can send me a minimal working example.

Best,
Chris
